items.title: Mahama urges African countries to strengthen mineral deals to retain more resource wealth
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has urged African countries to strengthen their negotiating capacity in the mining sector to ensure the continent derives greater economic benefits from its vast mineral resources. He said weak negotiations and the granting of extensive mining concessions to foreign companies have deprived African nations of a substantial share of the wealth generated from their natural resources, leaving many resource-rich communities struggling with poverty. Speaking at the Mining in Motion Conference on Monday, October 19, President Mahama identified the African Minerals Development Centre (AMDC) as a critical platform for helping countries on the continent negotiate better mining agreements, exchange geological information and build regional industries around mineral resources. He called on African Union member states that have yet to ratify the statutes establishing the centre to expedite the process and submit their instruments of ratification to the African Union. He also stressed the need for adequate funding, technical capacity and clear performance targets to enable the institution to deliver on its objectives. President Mahama argued that Africa’s continued inability to convert its mineral endowment into widespread prosperity was partly rooted in historical arrangements that favour external interests over the economic advancement of producing countries and their communities. “Poor negotiations and the award of large mineral concessions to foreign interests leave African nations with just a pittance of the wealth that is extracted from our soils. This results in massive financial outflows from the continent, while African countries and their communities grovel in misery,” he said. He maintained that a properly resourced AMDC could help African governments secure more favourable terms in mineral agreements and reduce the disproportionate flow of wealth out of the continent. Through stronger regional value chains, he said, African countries could retain more of the benefits from extraction by expanding local processing, industrial development and economic opportunities linked to their mineral resources.

items.title: FG targets N750trn stock market with NNPC, NLNG listing
items.description: •As SEC launches National Savings Scheme By Obas Esiedesa, Abuja The Federal Government (FG) has unveiled a 10-year plan to grow Nigeria’s capital market to N750 trillion by 2036, while calling for the listing of selected state-owned enterprises, including the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPC) and Nigeria LNG Limited (NLNG), on the Nigerian Exchange. This was disclosed by Vice President Kashim Shettima, while unveiling the Nigerian Capital Market Master Plan 2.0 at the National Capital Market Conference 2026 in Abuja on Monday, describing the market as a critical instrument for mobilising long-term financing for infrastructure and economic development. The plan, developed by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), targets expansion of the capital market from a baseline of about N250 trillion to N750 trillion over the next decade. Shettima said Nigeria’s capital market had recorded significant growth since the President Bola Tinubu administration assumed office in May 2023. The Vice President attributed the growth to reforms undertaken by the Federal Government, including the removal of petrol subsidy, unification of the foreign exchange market, tax reforms, bank recapitalisation and the enactment of the Investments and Securities Act 2025. He said the master plan would position the capital market at the centre of infrastructure financing, enabling governments and businesses to raise long-term funds locally rather than rely excessively on short-term or foreign borrowing. Shettima added that the plan would strengthen the bond market for state and subnational governments, broaden retail participation through technology and investor education, and provide businesses in agriculture, solid minerals and other sectors with opportunities to raise capital locally. The Vice President, who chairs the National Economic Council, said he would work with state governors to encourage responsible capital market financing through properly structured bonds, credible project pipelines and greater transparency. He said such financing could promote fiscal discipline and strengthen accountability in public spending, warning that policy reversals could undermine investor confidence and erode recent gains. However, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister for the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, said Nigeria should aim for a $1 trillion capital market within the next 10 years to support the country’s ambition of building a $1 trillion economy by 2030. He urged the government to accelerate the listing of selected state-owned enterprises, particularly NNPC and NLNG, arguing that making their shares available to investors would deepen the market, improve transparency and broaden public ownership of national assets. On the proposed listing of state-owned enterprises, Oyedele said the government would also introduce incentives to encourage privately owned Nigerian companies to list on the Nigerian Exchange rather than compel them to do so. “We cannot force them. We would encourage Nigerian private businesses to list. We will use incentives to attract them,” he said. Under the proposed master plan, the Minister said Nigeria would target an increase in equity market capitalisation from 33 per cent of gross domestic product to at least 60 per cent, while raising the number of listed companies from 146 to 250 and expanding retail investors from six million to 20 million. Other targets include more than tripling corporate bond issuance as a share of GDP, increasing Sukuk market penetration from 0.3 per cent to at least five per cent of GDP, and raising pension assets from six per cent to 16 per cent of GDP. Oyedele said Nigeria was also working to improve its standing among international investors, citing the country’s reinstatement in the FTSE Russell Frontier Market Index on September 21, 2026, and the inclusion of Nigerian government bonds in a new J.P. Morgan government bond index, with a weight of 7.4 per cent. He said the government was seeking a return to J.P. Morgan’s flagship government bond index and an eventual upgrade to emerging-market status. The Minister added that the government was targeting an investment-grade credit rating within three years, noting that this would require sustained reforms, improved market liquidity and reliable repatriation of foreign investors’ funds. As part of efforts to deepen domestic investment, Oyedele formally launched the National Savings Scheme, designed to provide Nigerians with regulated avenues to save and invest towards education, housing, business development and retirement. The Minister also announced plans to strengthen enforcement against Ponzi schemes through improved surveillance, social media monitoring and collaboration with law enforcement agencies. He added that the government was considering a fraud restitution mechanism to support victims. Speaking at the conference, the Director-General of the SEC, Dr Emomotimi Agama, said the master plan was designed to deepen market participation, expand investment products and strengthen the integrity and infrastructure of the capital market. He disclosed that the Project Steering Committee and the Capital Market Master Plan Implementation Committee would be inaugurated to oversee implementation. items.title: Mahama Ayariga calls for stronger local governance to ensure mining benefits communities
items.description: The Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, has called for stronger local governance, community participation and accountability in the mining sector to ensure that Africa’s mineral wealth translates into improved living conditions for its people. He said the continent’s abundant mineral resources presented significant opportunities for economic growth and sustainable development, but stressed the need for policies that ensure mining communities benefit meaningfully from the exploitation of resources in their localities. Mr Ayariga made the remarks after participating in the African Minerals Policy Forum’s Mining in Motion 2026 conference in Accra, which brought together stakeholders to discuss the future of Africa’s mining industry. The discussions focused on the theme, “Sovereignty as Practice: Strengthening African Bargaining Power and Delivering Local Benefits.” In a Facebook post on Monday, October 19, the minister highlighted the importance of ensuring that mineral resources contribute to national development and improve the livelihoods of people in mining communities. He noted that effective local governance structures, meaningful participation by affected communities and transparent management of mineral revenues were essential to ensuring that the benefits of mining reached the people most affected by extraction activities. Mr Ayariga’s remarks underscore the role of local authorities and community stakeholders in promoting responsible resource management and ensuring that mining activities support inclusive development. He maintained that strengthening accountability and local participation would be critical to building resilient communities and securing a sustainable future for Africa.

items.title: FG rolls out 2 major benefits to shield retirees from poverty, ill health
items.description: •As PenCom kicks off maiden Pension week October 26 By Victor Ahiuma-Young The Federal Government, through the National Pension Commission, PenCom, is set to introduce two landmark initiatives aimed at protecting retirees from poverty and ill health as Nigeria prepares to mark its maiden National Pension Week from October 26 to 30, 2026. The initiatives, PenCare, a retiree healthcare programme, and the Minimum Pension Guarantee, are expected to strengthen social protection for eligible retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, CPS, addressing concerns over access to essential healthcare and inadequate retirement income. Director-General of PenCom, Ms. Omolola Oloworaran, disclosed this in Lagos, where she announced plans for the nationwide pension week and outlined the commission’s priorities for improving retirement security. According to Oloworaran, the two initiatives will mark a significant step in translating pension reforms into tangible benefits for Nigerian retirees. “Later this month, during National Pension Week, two historic commitments will move from reform to reality,” she said. She explained that the first initiative, PenCare, would provide eligible low-income retirees with access to essential healthcare services at no cost, beginning with 30,000 beneficiaries. “It will give eligible low-income retirees access to essential healthcare at no cost to them, beginning with 30,000 retirees,” the PenCom Director General stated. Emphasising the importance of healthcare in retirement, Oloworaran declared: “No Nigerian should retire into poverty. And no Nigerian should retire into ill health.” The second initiative, the Minimum Pension Guarantee, is designed to establish a minimum level of pension protection for eligible retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme. Oloworaran said the programme would activate a safeguard provided for in pension law for more than a decade, ensuring that eligible retirees would not fall below a prescribed minimum pension level. “For the first time, a protection that has stood in our pension law for more than a decade will take effect. It will set a floor beneath which no eligible retiree under the Contributory Pension Scheme will fall,” she said. She added that the guarantee would be particularly important for retirees whose accumulated savings might otherwise leave them struggling to meet basic needs. “For the retiree with the smallest savings, that floor is the difference between hardship and dignity,” she said. The Director General described the planned rollout as part of a broader effort to make pension reforms deliver measurable improvements in the lives of retirees, noting that the commission had already implemented several measures to improve pension payments and access to retirement benefits. “Seven historic firsts delivered. Two more within weeks. In a single administration,” she said, referring to the reforms highlighted in her address. National Pension Week, scheduled for October 26 to 30, is expected to provide a platform for greater public awareness of pension rights, retirement planning and the need to expand pension coverage across the country. Oloworaran said the commission would use the occasion to encourage Nigerians, particularly young workers, to take a greater interest in their retirement savings and understand the benefits available under the pension system. “To young Nigerians: start the conversation early. Know your Pension Fund Administrator. Read your statement. Ask where your contributions are,” she urged. She stressed that retirement security depended not only on regulatory reforms but also on workers’ awareness, employers’ compliance and the timely remittance of pension contributions. The commission also called on state governments and private-sector employers to strengthen pension compliance and expand coverage, particularly among workers who remain outside formal retirement savings arrangements. The planned introduction of PenCare and the Minimum Pension Guarantee comes amid continuing efforts to improve the adequacy of retirement benefits and provide greater protection for vulnerable pensioners. For PenCom, the central objective of the initiatives is to ensure that retirement offers Nigerians greater financial security and access to essential services, rather than exposing them to hardship after years of service. As the maiden National Pension Week approaches, attention is expected to focus on the implementation of the two programmes, the eligibility criteria for beneficiaries and the arrangements for delivering the promised protections to retirees. items.title: Ghana Card replacement now available at NIA Prestige 24/7 Centres
items.description: The National Identification Authority (NIA) has extended its Ghana Card replacement service to selected service centres across the country, alongside a new online application option for Ghanaians living abroad. The Executive Secretary of the Authority, Wisdom Koku Deku, announced the development in a Facebook post on Monday, October 19, 2026, confirming that applicants could now access the replacement service through the NIA’s online portal and designated centres. The service is available at all four operational Prestige 24/7 Centres in Labone, Sakumono, Bantama and Suame. The Authority says the Amakom Prestige 24/7 Centre will begin offering the service soon. Applicants who prefer to visit a Premium Centre can also access the replacement service through the online portal at register.nia.gov.gh. The online service also allows Ghanaians living in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, the Netherlands, Spain, the United Arab Emirates, France, Italy, Belgium, Germany and Denmark to apply for replacement Ghana Cards without travelling to Ghana. The expansion is expected to provide additional options for applicants seeking replacement cards, particularly Ghanaians living outside the country. Mr Deku further indicated that an update service would be added to the portal soon, suggesting that the NIA intends to expand the range of services available through its digital platform. The Authority reaffirmed its commitment to providing efficient and accessible services to the public under its slogan, “Providing Future Solutions Now.”

items.title: What Is Wrong With Us: When a peaceful election quietly becomes a sad ending for honest businesses
items.description: By Ing. Prof. Douglas Boateng, Chartered Director UK | Chartered Engineer UK | Fellow, Institute of Directors UK | Fellow, Ghana Institution of Engineering | Governance, Industrialisation and Supply Chain Strategist | Founder, Boardroom Governance Summit | Founder and Scriber, NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) Ghana’s democratic transitions rightly inspire admiration. It is therefore all the more unfortunate, and deeply worrying, that each change of government can leave committed entrepreneurs unpaid, loyal workers uncertain and promising enterprises struggling to survive. Twenty Years to Build, One Election to Unsettle Imagine spending twenty years building a company. You employ engineers, accountants, technicians, drivers and young graduates, invest in equipment and training, and borrow from a bank to execute a government contract won through proper procurement. The work is completed, the institution accepts delivery and your invoice is submitted. Then an election takes place, a new administration assumes office, and the payment that should have settled your obligations suddenly becomes uncertain while your contract is reviewed. The bank, however, does not recognise political transitions as a reason to suspend interest, your employees do not stop eating because a new minister has been sworn in, and the electricity company has shown no inclination to supply free power while the state decides whether it approves of the political colour of your company’s owner. A Democracy We Celebrate, an Economy We Unsettle Ghana deserves genuine pride in its democratic record. Since 2008 it has witnessed peaceful transfers of power in 2009, 2017 and 2025, demonstrating that political authority belongs to citizens rather than to permanent rulers. Yet democracy becomes economically expensive when each change of government ushers in a commercial winter, in which legitimate obligations of the state are frozen, questioned and delayed, and businesses perceived to have worked with the outgoing administration find themselves under a cloud of suspicion. We change governments through the ballot box, but too often we behave as though legitimate businesses must also change their identities, loyalties and commercial histories. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) warns that “a nation cannot build a sustainable private sector when every election threatens to become a commercial earthquake.” Scrutiny Is a Duty, Not a Weapon None of this suggests that incoming governments should accept every contract signed by their predecessors. Fraud must be investigated, inflated contracts challenged, unlawful procurement punished, and no undelivered work should ever be paid for merely because someone presents an invoice. After the Finance Minister announced in April 2025 that contractor payments would await an audit of outstanding claims, the Ghana News Agency reported in March 2026 that of roughly GH¢68.7 billion examined, GH¢45.4 billion was validated, GH¢8.1 billion was rejected for irregularities and GH¢13.3 billion required further justification. Those figures expose two truths that must be held together: the state must never pay fraudulent claims, and it must never destroy legitimate businesses while hunting for fraudulent ones. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) counsels that “when dishonesty is found among some contractors, justice requires identifying the dishonest, not suffocating everybody.” An Audit Without a Clock Becomes a Sentence The same figures carry a quieter message, for roughly two thirds of the claims examined were found to be valid, which means that many honest firms waited for money they had genuinely earned. An audit is a necessary instrument of public accountability, but it must come with deadlines, transparent procedures, a fair opportunity for contractors to respond and a mechanism that releases verified payments promptly, even while disputed portions are resolved. Without those safeguards, a tool designed to protect public money can inadvertently destroy the very enterprises that generate the taxes, jobs and growth on which public money depends. The Bank Never Changes Government Consider an illustrative engineering firm owed GH¢10 million for completed and certified work, financed by a loan costing 25 percent a year. If the full amount remains outstanding for twelve months, simple interest alone consumes GH¢2.5 million, and when the state eventually pays the original invoice without compensation for delay, the firm has received its money while losing a quarter of its value. Some contracts do provide for interest, but no supplier can assume that interest will accrue automatically on a delayed public invoice. In effect, the state enjoys an interest free loan funded by businesses borrowing at commercial rates to deliver public services, which is not industrialisation but the quiet transfer of fiscal risk from government to its most dependable partners. When One Invoice Waits, Many Families Wait A contractor is never simply an individual collecting government money. Behind every company stand employees, subcontractors, transport operators, insurers, equipment suppliers and the households they support, so that one delayed payment becomes unpaid wages, reduced spending, distressed loans, repossessed equipment, departing skills and falling tax receipts. The World Bank’s most recent Enterprise Survey of Ghana identified access to finance as the single obstacle firms cited most frequently, and one can imagine what happens when scarce, expensive credit meets unpredictable public payment. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) observes that “a government that delays payment to a productive business may save cash today while destroying tomorrow’s jobs, taxes and investment.” When Party Colours Become Credit Ratings There is a further, more delicate dimension. In polarised political environments, an entrepreneur who lawfully won a contract under one administration may be presumed to belong to its party, and a photograph with a former minister can become a commercial liability. It would be unfair to claim that every delayed payment or contract review is politically motivated, and each case deserves proper investigation. Yet even the perception that commercial survival depends on political proximity is corrosive, because it rewards networking over competence, encourages firms to seek protection rather than productivity and tempts entrepreneurs to fund political relationships as insurance against future exclusion. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) reminds us that “when a company must change political colours to survive, the nation is no longer rewarding enterprise but political camouflage.” No company should need a political godfather to be paid for lawful work, and no political connection should protect a company that has defrauded the state. A Global Problem With Known Remedies Ghana is hardly alone. Nigeria has wrestled with disputed public liabilities and stalled infrastructure payments, while South Africa’s Treasury rules require public institutions to settle valid invoices within thirty days, an obligation still too often honoured in the breach where small businesses are concerned. The European Union’s Late Payment Directive generally obliges public authorities to pay within thirty days and entitles creditors to statutory interest and a fixed compensation for recovery costs when they do not. Whatever their imperfections, the principle they embody is clear: a public institution must never treat delayed payment as a free source of working capital. Governments Pass, the Republic Remains The principle Ghana must recover is constitutional as much as economic. A government serves for a limited term, but the state continues; a minister changes, but the ministry remains; a president departs, but the Republic endures, and lawful obligations of the state do not evaporate because a different party occupies the seat of government. Contracts may lawfully be terminated and unlawful agreements challenged, but a properly executed and legally enforceable commitment cannot become optional with each electoral cycle. Investors read these signals carefully, pricing political risk into every bid or avoiding public work altogether, and in the end it is the taxpayer who pays the premium. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) cautions that “political power is temporary, but the credibility of the state must survive every transition.” Both Sides of the Ledger Must Be Honest Responsibility does not rest with incoming governments alone. Outgoing administrations must not commit future taxpayers to spending without authorisation, budgetary provision or a proper assessment of value for money, and the International Monetary Fund’s review of Ghana’s 2024 fiscal slippages pointed to commitments made outside established financial management systems and spending pressures ahead of elections. Public officials must not certify work that was never done, and contractors must not inflate invoices and then demand payment simply because a document bears an official signature. The solution therefore has two inseparable halves: stop creating unlawful liabilities, and pay lawful liabilities predictably, for one without the other will never restore confidence. Rules That Outlast Elections Ghana should enact a binding prompt payment framework under which certified and undisputed invoices are settled within thirty days, subject to narrowly defined exceptions, with interest accruing automatically on qualifying public obligations when that deadline is missed. A digital national register of contracts and payments should record approvals, values, certified work and outstanding balances. Government commitments should be independently reconciled before and after every election, so that no incoming administration discovers billions in undisclosed obligations and no contractor must prove all over again that work was completed. Disputed claims deserve independent and affordable resolution within fixed timelines, the undisputed portion of any invoice should be paid without delay, and ministries that repeatedly create unfunded commitments or withhold verified payments without lawful justification should face institutional and personal accountability. Banks can then finance verified government receivables against transparent payment schedules rather than political assurances. The Mindset Shift That Must Come First Rules alone will not suffice without a change of heart. Political leaders, public servants, citizens and the media must learn to see competent local businesses as national assets rather than party trophies, judging every contractor by legality, performance and value for money, never by perceived political association. An inclusive economy is one in which a firm can serve successive governments of different persuasions with the same professionalism, and be paid with the same reliability, because its loyalty is to the Republic and its contracts are with the state. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) observes that “a nation cannot build industries for fifty years with a political memory of only four.” What Is Wrong With Us? We celebrate peaceful transfers of power while overlooking the economic wreckage that sometimes surrounds them, praise entrepreneurs while exposing them to unpredictable payment, and speak passionately about growth led by the private sector while allowing the state to become an unreliable customer. We ask businesses to create jobs, pay taxes and train young people, and then expect them to survive prolonged uncertainty without financial protection, which is curious arithmetic for any nation that dreams of industrialisation. NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom) offers the final reflection: “When governments change, leaders, policies and priorities may change, but the state’s duty to honour legitimate commitments must never change.” A country should be able to change its government without forcing its businesses to restart their lives, and until we accept that this is not a favour to contractors but a foundation of economic civilisation, we must keep asking ourselves the same uncomfortable question: what is wrong with us? ABOUT THE AUTHOR Ing. Professor Douglas Boateng is a pioneering international industrial, manufacturing and production systems engineer, governance strategist and Pan-African thought leader whose work continues to influence boardroom thinking, supply chain transformation and industrialisation strategy across the continent and beyond. As Africa’s first appointed Professor Extraordinaire in Supply Chain Management, he has long championed the integration of procurement, value chain development, industrialisation and governance into national and continental development agendas. An International Chartered Director and Chartered Engineer, he has received numerous lifetime achievement awards and authored several authoritative books. He is the scribe of the globally acclaimed NyansaKasa (Words of Wisdom). His work rests on the conviction that Africa’s transformation — and the protection of its children — will come through deliberate action, strong institutions and leaders willing to build for generations they will never meet. © 2026 Ing. items.title: NIA opens online Ghana Card replacement service to Ghanaians in 11 countries
items.description: The National Identification Authority (NIA) has introduced an online Ghana Card replacement service for Ghanaians living in 11 countries, allowing them to replace their cards without travelling to Ghana. The Executive Secretary of the NIA, Wisdom Koku Deku, announced the development in a Facebook post on Monday, October 19, 2026, saying the service had been added to the Authority’s online application portal. The service is available to Ghanaians living in the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, the Netherlands, Spain, the United Arab Emirates, France, Italy, Belgium, Germany and Denmark. Applicants can access the service through the NIA’s online portal at register.nia.gov.gh, providing an alternative for Ghanaians abroad who need replacement cards. Mr Deku also announced that the service was available at all Prestige 24/7 Centres in Labone, Sakumono, Bantama and Suame. The Amakom Prestige 24/7 Centre is expected to begin offering the service soon. He added that applicants who prefer to visit a Premium Centre could also access the replacement service through the online portal. An update service is expected to be introduced soon as part of efforts to expand the Authority’s digital services. The NIA says it remains committed to delivering efficient and accessible services to Ghanaians.

items.title: US bars IT firm from sponsoring green cards, imposes $2m settlement
items.description: WASHINGTON: The United States has barred California-based technology company Cloudera Inc. from participating in the employment-based green card process for two years and secured a $2 million settlement over allegations that it discriminated against qualified American workers. The settlement was announced jointly by the US Department of Justice and the Department of Labour. It resolves a lawsuit filed by the Justice Department in April, alleging that Cloudera violated the Immigration and Nationality Act by discriminating against American workers while recruiting for seven positions under the Permanent Labour Certification, or PERM, programme. Under the settlement, Cloudera will establish a $1.4m fund to compensate qualified US workers who tried to apply for the positions but were not given fair consideration. The company will also pay $600,000 in civil penalties to the US government. “There are no exceptions: the Justice Department will hold accountable employers who discriminate against US workers,” Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division said. The warning has wider implications for future employment-based green card applications. Employers found to have discriminated against qualified American workers could face penalties and restrictions on their ability to sponsor foreign employees, potentially disrupting the permanent residency plans of those workers. The Cloudera case demonstrates how enforcement action against an employer can directly affect foreign professionals seeking green cards through company sponsorship. The company will also face enhanced monitoring, revised compliance procedures and reporting requirements designed to prevent future violations. The two-year debarment follows an earlier suspension of Cloudera’s PERM processing by the Labour Department. During the debarment period, the company cannot participate in the PERM programme to sponsor foreign workers for employment-based green cards. The PERM programme is generally the first major step when a US employer seeks to sponsor a foreign worker for an employment-based green card under the EB-2 or EB-3 categories. Employers must normally demonstrate that no qualified, willing and available American workers could be found for the position and that employing the foreign worker would not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed US workers. According to the allegations, Cloudera’s recruitment for seven positions did not give qualified American workers a fair opportunity to compete. Applicants were reportedly directed to an email address that did not accept messages from outside senders, potentially preventing them from submitting applications. The decision is relevant to Indian and Pakistani professionals seeking US permanent residency through employer sponsorship, but it does not impose a general ban on green cards for nationals of either country. Cloudera-sponsored applications could face disruption. Employees whose green card cases depend on the company’s labour certification may face delays or need to explore lawful alternatives, depending on their individual circumstances and the stage of their cases. The debarment does not, by itself, establish that every existing green card application sponsored by Cloudera will be cancelled. The settlement also underscores the potential consequences for employers that fail to provide American workers a genuine opportunity to compete for jobs. Depending on the findings and enforcement action in an individual case, such employers could face financial penalties, compliance requirements or restrictions on their participation in employment-based immigration programmes. However, the wider immigration rules remain unchanged. The settlement does not alter employment-based visa eligibility, annual numerical limits or country-specific visa allocation rules. The Justice Department said the Cloudera settlement was the 14th since it relaunched its Protecting US Workers Initiative in 2025. The initiative targets employers accused of unlawfully favouring foreign workers holding temporary employment visas over qualified American workers. The case underscores the importance of fair recruitment practices in the green card sponsorship process. Employers must provide American workers a genuine opportunity to apply before seeking labour certification for foreign employees. On October 8, the Trump administration froze some green-card filings by Microsoft, Adobe and major IT outsourcers and opened probes into nine elite universities, widening a visa crackdown it said targets fraud and American job losses.

items.title: Mahama Ayariga highlights need for African unity in mining to secure local benefits
items.description: The Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, has emphasised the need for African countries to adopt coordinated approaches to mineral resource management to ensure that the continent’s natural wealth delivers lasting economic and social benefits. He said Africa’s mineral endowment could serve as a major driver of development if countries prioritised policies that promote responsible extraction, strengthen local participation and ensure that revenue from mining contributes to improving the welfare of citizens. Mr Ayariga participated in the African Minerals Policy Forum’s Mining in Motion 2026 conference in Accra, where policymakers and other industry stakeholders discussed strategies for strengthening Africa’s position in the global mining sector. The forum was held under the theme, “Sovereignty as Practice: Strengthening African Bargaining Power and Delivering Local Benefits.” Reflecting on the discussions in a Facebook post on Monday, October 19, the minister said the continent needed to focus on ensuring that mineral wealth supports national development and improves livelihoods. He highlighted local governance, community participation and accountability in mineral revenue management as important components of this process. For Mr Ayariga, the management of mineral resources must go beyond extraction and revenue generation to deliver tangible benefits to communities. Stronger local institutions and greater community involvement, he noted, can help ensure that mining contributes to sustainable development and creates better prospects for future generations across Africa.

items.title: Rubio heads to India for 'trade diplomacy'
items.description: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio heads to India on Tuesday for his second official visit to the country this year, as he pursues an Asian tour blending diplomacy and trade. After a trip to Uzbekistan, where he called for stronger partnerships with Central Asian countries, Rubio will head to Mumbai to hold talks with Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar and meet business leaders. The top US diplomat visited New Delhi and Kolkata in May, while also touring the Taj Mahal and meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. No meeting with Modi is planned during this trip, which will also take Rubio to Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, a port and stronghold of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance conglomerate — including its key refinery, the world’s largest. He is also expected to lay a wreath in memory of the 2008 Mumbai attacks that killed 166 people. Rubio’s visit comes as the two countries struggle to finalise a trade deal that has been a source of repeated tensions. Speaking in Samarkand on Monday, he said Washington and New Delhi were “very close” to an agreement. However, the prospects of securing a deal during this visit appeared slim. US President Donald Trump’s tariff war launched in April last year has added to friction over India’s imports of Russian oil and warming ties between Washington and Pakistan, India’s arch-rival. Asked about temporary US sanctions waivers for Russian oil , of which India is a major importer, Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors “including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies”. “You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue,” he said. The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods. But days later, the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect. The two sides have been negotiating since. Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman this month described the talks as having reached “a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult”.

items.title: Mahama warns against sacrificing rivers and forests for mineral wealth
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called for stronger environmental and social protections in Ghana’s mining industry, stressing that the exploitation of mineral resources must not come at the expense of communities, workers and the environment. Addressing the Mining in Motion Conference on Monday, October 19, the President emphasised the need for responsible mining practices that balance economic development with the protection of natural resources and the welfare of people living in mining areas. He said Ghana’s rivers, forests and farmlands were valuable national assets that must be preserved rather than destroyed in the pursuit of mineral wealth. He also called for mining communities to receive a fair share of the benefits generated from mineral extraction, while urging mining companies to prioritise workers’ safety and ensure that lands affected by mining activities are properly reclaimed and rehabilitated. “Mineral development must safeguard the lives of our people, their livelihoods, and their environments. Our rivers, forests, and farmlands are part of our wealth. Communities must share fairly in the benefits, and workers must be protected, and mined lands must be reclaimed and rehabilitated,” President Mahama said. He further underscored the importance of transparency and accountability in the management of mineral revenues, insisting that proceeds from the sector must translate into tangible benefits for citizens.

items.title: UG secures 96,000 Gemini AI licences for staff and students
items.description: The University of Ghana (UG) has partnered with Google to secure more than 96,000 licences for “Gemini for Education” to boost digital skills, research, and teaching across the institution. The initiative aims to equip students and faculty with Artificial Intelligence (AI) competencies demanded by modern employers as industries redefine graduate employability standards. Speaking at a two-day training workshop on Gemini AI, Mr Emmanuel Adeniyi, Higher Education Lead for West and Central Africa at Google, noted that industry expectations have evolved significantly, making AI proficiency a key requirement for job seekers. “More and more employers are asking and redefining what an employable graduate looks like. For many of them, they are prioritising students who show evidence of competencies in Artificial Intelligence.” Mr Adeniyi said. “So I think it is important, as you see with many universities like the University of Ghana, to ensure that students are supported to navigate the era of Artificial Intelligence.” He explained that the Gemini platform was specifically built with learning science in mind and includes enterprise-grade data protection to safeguard institutional information. During the session, faculty and administrative staff drawn from various colleges and the central administration received practical training on integrating AI tools effectively and responsibly into academic and administrative workflows. Addressing the participants, Professor Sandow Mark Yidana, Provost of the College of Basic and Applied Sciences, said the partnership aligned directly with the University’s strategic vision. He urged the trained staff to serve as AI champions within their respective units and train other colleagues and students. Professor Yidana, however, cautioned that the adoption of generative AI must be guided by ethical considerations and academic integrity. “As we embrace Artificial Intelligence, we must remain mindful of the associated responsibilities.” Professor Yidana stressed. “AI-generated information must be critically evaluated, while issues related to data protection, intellectual property, respect for confidentiality, and academic integrity must be carefully managed in line with our AI policy.” He added that UG remained committed to driving innovation without compromising its high academic standards. Background The University of Ghana deal is part of a broader national and continental rollout of Google’s AI education tools. In June 2026, Ghana’s Ministry of Education signed a Memorandum of Understanding with Google for Education during the Education World Forum in London to integrate AI into Ghanaian classrooms, move beyond basic digital literacy and build AI fluency. The agreement provides for curriculum-aligned content, teacher training and zero-rated access to ensure equitable access, including in rural areas. Google is also working with UG and the Ghana Digital Innovation Hub (GDI Hub) to develop speech recognition for Ghanaian local languages, including Twi, Ewe, Dagbani and Hausa, to improve accessibility in education and digital services. The rollout complements the company’s pan-African student offer. In August 2026, Google expanded free 12-month access to Google AI Plus, including Gemini Advanced, NotebookLM, Veo 3 for video generation, and 2TB of storage, for eligible higher-education students in 27 African countries, including Ghana. The offer, which requires verification through SheerID, provides tools such as the Student Hub for organising studies, study notebooks that turn lecture notes into quizzes, interactive visualisations, and Deep Research. Within Ghana, UG is the second major public university to adopt Gemini at scale. The Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) announced in August 2026 that it had secured 95,000 Google Workspace for Education Fundamentals licences through its E-Learning Centre, led by Ing. Prof. Emmanuel Kofi Akowuah. KNUST’s deployment uses Single Sign-On with existing university credentials and is provided under Google’s Core Services framework, meaning institutional data is not used to train public AI models. Training for faculty began in September 2026, with a physical Gemini Academy scheduled for November. The initiative aligns with Google’s partnership with the African Union Commission to bring Gemini for Education and NotebookLM to universities across all 55 member states, with a target of training at least 150,000 students and faculty by 2027. For UG, the partnership is governed by the University’s AI Policy, which covers all use of third-party AI platforms, including ChatGPT, Gemini, GitHub Copilot, and Grammarly, in teaching, learning, research, and administration, and emphasises data protection, intellectual property, and academic integrity.

items.title: Ghana reviewing revised US health funding deal after rejecting initial proposal – Mintah Akandoh
items.description: The government is considering a revised health financing proposal from the United States after declining to accept an earlier version over concerns about its implications for Ghana’s sovereignty, regulatory authority and national interests. Health Minister Kwabena Mintah Akandoh says the government will not rush into an agreement simply because Ghana needs international support for its health sector. He insists that any partnership must respect the country’s laws and provide a framework based on mutual respect rather than dependency. The initial proposal was subjected to scrutiny by the Ministry of Health before being presented to Cabinet, where concerns about some of its provisions were considered. The proposed arrangement was expected to replace health funding previously provided through the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). One major concern involved a provision that would reportedly exempt US pharmaceutical products covered by the agreement from verification or certification by Ghana’s Food and Drugs Authority (FDA). The minister questioned the implications of such an arrangement for the country’s ability to regulate medicines entering its health system. The government also raised questions about requirements for sharing health information with the US. Mr Akandoh maintained that the distinction between individual records and aggregated data did not remove the need for careful scrutiny, given the importance of protecting information and ensuring that data-sharing arrangements serve Ghana’s interests. The minister further expressed reservations about the framing of the proposed compact, drawing attention to the US administration’s “America First” policy. He argued that Ghana must similarly place its own priorities at the centre of negotiations and ensure that external partnerships do not undermine its national objectives. In an interview with Channel One TV on Monday, October 19, Mr Akandoh said the government had documented its concerns and taken them to Cabinet in accordance with President John Dramani Mahama’s directive that matters requiring further consideration be referred to the collective decision-making body. He said the Ministry of Health and the Foreign Affairs Ministry were subsequently tasked with communicating Ghana’s position to their American counterparts. The US has since submitted another memorandum of understanding (MoU), which is being examined before it is sent to Cabinet for a decision. Mr Akandoh stressed that Ghana’s need for development partners would not compel the government to accept conditions it considered unsuitable. “No, I’m never under any pressure. Trust us to take the best decision in the interest of the country,” he said. Emphasising the government’s preferred approach to international cooperation, he added: “We need partnership, but we need partnership with respect and dignity. So these fragmentations and tendencies and promises of partnership — no, we will have to move from dependency to dignity, from fragmentation to solidarity.” The latest development follows President Mahama’s disclosure that Washington had requested further engagement with Accra to revise or remove contentious provisions of the proposed agreement. The government says the revised document remains under consideration, with no final decision on whether to proceed with the arrangement until Cabinet has reviewed it.

items.title: Quality and integrity must define Ghanaian brands – Prof. Stephen Adei
items.description: Professor Stephen Adei, Patron of the Chartered Institute of Marketing, Ghana (CIMG), has urged marketing practitioners to help build competitive Ghanaian brands that deliver quality products and services. Speaking at the 37th CIMG Annual National Marketing Performance Awards in Accra, he said the success of businesses in the era of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) would depend on their ability to create valuable and trustworthy products and services that meet consumers’ needs. “Technology may change how brands reach consumers, but it does not change the basis of a lasting business relationship: trust. Access to technology alone will not guarantee success. The real opportunity lies in using innovation to create products and services that people need, value and trust,” he said. Prof. Adei added that customers remained loyal to brands that kept their promises, investors supported credible businesses, and international buyers maintained relationships with suppliers who delivered consistently. The CIMG Awards recognise brands, organisations, institutions and professionals whose outstanding marketing contributions supported Ghana’s economic growth. The ceremony, held on Saturday at the Labadi Beach Hotel in Accra, was on the theme: “Brand Ghana Reimagined: Trust, Innovation and Growth in the AI Economy.” Prof. Adei said businesses and marketing professionals had a responsibility to promote Ghana’s reputation through quality products, reliable service delivery, business integrity and innovation. “Every Ghanaian business that delivers quality strengthens our national reputation, and every exporter who honours a contract builds confidence in our country. Poor quality and broken promises undermine it,” he said. He noted that credibility had become even more valuable in an AI-driven marketplace, where content could be generated at unprecedented speed. “We must make authenticity, quality assurance and professional integrity the defining features of Ghanaian enterprise,” he added. Prof. Adei described trust as an economic asset and emphasised the role of marketing in connecting production to demand and communicating the distinctive value of Ghanaian products and services. He called for stronger collaboration among industry players, professional institutions, educational establishments and government, while urging the CIMG to continue helping businesses recognise marketing as a strategic investment rather than merely a promotional expense. He commended the CIMG for strengthening professional standards and urged award winners to uphold the values and practices that earned them recognition. Mr Michael Abbiw, National President of the CIMG, also urged businesses to embrace artificial intelligence while maintaining customer trust to achieve sustainable growth. “The brands that win the AI economy will be the brands that are believed. Technology gives us speed, not credibility. Credibility is built the old way, by keeping promises, one customer at a time,” he said. Mr Abbiw stressed that trust and innovation must underpin business growth, warning that prioritising growth without those foundations could undermine long-term value. “Trust first, innovation second, and growth follows from both. Reverse the order, and you get fast growth that collapses at the first scandal, innovation that frightens the customers it was meant to serve, and growth that creates no lasting value,” he said. He encouraged businesses and marketers to use AI tools with sound personal and ethical judgement, noting that consumers continued to demand better products and services. “Adopt AI because it solves problems, creates value and serves customers better, not because it is fashionable,” he said. He urged CIMG members to enrol in the institute’s short course on AI in Marketing. Mr Abbiw further called on corporate boards to recognise marketing as a strategic management function and give it a voice at the highest level of decision-making, citing its role in providing insights into customers, markets, competitors and brand reputation. The ceremony recognised outstanding performance across 55 award categories, with new companies also inducted into the CIMG Hall of Fame. Madam Abena Amoah, Managing Director of the Ghana Stock Exchange, was named Marketing Woman of the Year, in recognition of her contribution to marketing and leadership in Ghana’s financial sector. Mr Salem Kalmoni, Managing Director of Japan Motors, was named Marketing Man of the Year for his contribution to marketing and business leadership. Madam Mavis Frimpong, the Head of Corporate Communications, Marketing and Brands at Consolidated Bank Ghana Limited, received the Marketing Practitioner of the Year award. Thomasina Tetey, Import Sales Manager at MSC Mediterranean Shipping Company, was named Marketing Student of the Year. The Multimedia Group won four awards, including Media Organisation of the Year (2025), Media News Portal of the Year, Radio Programme of the Year for Drive Time on Joy, and New Media Campaign of the Year for its #NoToGalamsey campaign. The CIMG is Ghana’s sole chartered authority and professional body mandated to set standards, certify, register and regulate marketing practice in the country.

items.title: Investors push for Ghana’s return to global capital markets; government says no rush
items.description: Some offshore investors and fund managers are pressing Ghana to return to the international capital markets, citing improving economic conditions, credit rating upgrades and stronger international reserves. The calls emerged during investor engagements at the IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, including sessions attended by Joy Business. The issue also featured prominently at private meetings organised by international banks, where investors expressed interest in Ghana raising funds through bonds and syndicated loans. Reasons for the push For some investors, Ghana’s improving economic stability and the Bank of Ghana’s reserve build-up make the country an increasingly attractive investment destination. Others point to Ghana’s decision to pursue a non-financing Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) programme with the IMF, which they believe could help sustain fiscal discipline and protect recent economic gains. “With Ghana being under this PCI Programme, we don’t see things deteriorating or Ghana departing from the current economic gains soon,” one fund manager told Joy Business. Some investors are also seeking to diversify their portfolios and secure higher returns than those available in the United States. According to views expressed during the engagements, a Ghanaian Eurobond could offer investors an average yield of about 8%, compared with returns of around 5% or lower on investments in the US market. Such a yield would, however, represent a borrowing cost for Ghana. Another investor told Joy Business that, despite lingering concerns following Ghana’s debt default, the safeguards associated with the proposed PCI programme could help reduce the risk of another default. Addressing investors at one of the meetings, Bank of Ghana Governor Dr Johnson Asiama said the central bank would continue taking the necessary monetary policy measures to support currency stability and keep inflation low, despite external threats. Government’s response The Technical Advisor to the Finance Minister, Dr Theo Achampong, confirmed that calls for a return to international borrowing had been part of the government’s engagements with international banks. Speaking on PM Express Business Edition in Bangkok, he stressed that the government was in no rush to return to the international capital markets. “We want to continue stabilising things for now, build strong international reserves,” he said. “As we speak, there is no motivation to go to the international capital market.” Dr Achampong said the government’s focus was on improving Ghana’s credit ratings to secure investment-grade status. “When you look at our borrowing needs over the one year, the capital market is not an option,” he added. Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson has also maintained that borrowing from international capital markets is outside the government’s financing plans for 2026. Speaking at a joint press conference with a visiting IMF mission during the latest review of the Extended Credit Facility programme, he said any decision to return would be communicated to Ghanaians. “We are not in a hurry to go onto the international capital markets, and if we find a need to go to the international capital markets, we will accordingly inform the people of Ghana,” he said. The minister added that the 2026 Budget made no provision for financing from the international capital markets, effectively taking that option off the table for the year. IMF urges Ghana to rebuild investor confidence The IMF has urged Ghana to prioritise rebuilding investor confidence and improving its credit rating before returning to international capital markets. Speaking on Channel One TV, the IMF Resident Representative in Ghana, Dr Adrian Alter, said the immediate priority should be to consolidate the gains from debt restructuring and strengthen domestic financing capacity. He said Ghana’s debt position had improved significantly under the IMF-supported programme, with the latest Debt Sustainability Analysis moving the country from a high to a moderate risk of debt distress. According to Dr Alter, central government debt had declined to about 45% of gross domestic product, a level the Fund had initially projected Ghana would reach only by 2034. Professor Quartey cautions against a hasty return The Director of the Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER), Professor Peter Quartey, has also cautioned the government against a hasty return to international capital markets following Ghana’s debt restructuring. He called for a measured approach to borrowing, particularly through Eurobonds, warning that excessive reliance on external debt could undermine long-term economic stability. Professor Quartey made the remarks during his inaugural lecture at the Ghana Academy of Arts and Sciences on the theme, “Debt, Investment, and Growth in Ghana: Did We Borrow to Consume?”

items.title: TVET is Ghana’s transformation spine, driving force of 24-hour economy – Nana Oye
items.description: Nana Oye Bampoe Addo, the Deputy Chief of Staff in charge of Administration, has described Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) as central to Ghana’s economic transformation and growth, emphasising the critical role of industry in developing a skilled workforce. She said TVET was a key driver of the Government’s 24-hour economy agenda, which sought to make Ghana more productive, self-reliant and inclusive. The government, the Ghana TVET Service, industry and development partners were working together to reform the sector and maximise its contribution to national development, she said. Madam Bampo Addo made the remarks on Wednesday, October 14, during the opening of the three-day National TVET Week 2026 Policy Dialogue, organised by the Ghana TVET Service as part of activities marking the 10th anniversary of Ghana TVET Week. The dialogue was held on the theme: “Resetting TVET: Powering Ghana’s Industrial and Economic Transformation.” The event brought together industry leaders, heads of technical institutions, tutors, students, officials of the Ghana TVET Service, Members of Parliament, policymakers, academics, private-sector representatives, development partners, and civil society organisations. Madam Bampoe Addo said President John Mahama had set a target of increasing TVET enrolment from 11 per cent to 20 per cent to strengthen the sector’s contribution to the 24-hour economy through skills development and technical training. She said progress had been made towards that goal, with 70,000 learners enrolled in public TVET institutions in 2026. She also cited a pass rate of 75 per cent in the 2025 Certificate Tool Examination and nearly 35,000 learners participating in workplace experience learning. “Over 11,000 apprenticeship certificates have been issued, and about 60 Ghana Education Trust Fund (GETFund) projects are underway. This is a season of reset in TVET in Ghana,” Madam Bampo Addo said. The Deputy Chief of Staff also highlighted the importance of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into TVET programmes to equip learners with relevant skills for the evolving world of work. She noted that the Government launched the Ghana National Artificial Intelligence Strategy in April 2026, with the ambition of positioning Ghana as a leading hub for AI in West Africa and across the continent by 2035. She therefore urged TVET institutions to incorporate AI into their training programmes to enhance learners’ competencies and prepare them for emerging opportunities in the labour market. Dr Eric Kofi Adzroe, the Director-General of the Ghana TVET Service, called for TVET to be placed at the centre of Ghana’s industrial and economic transformation. He said sustainable industrialisation, competitive manufacturing, modern agriculture and the creation of quality jobs depended on a skilled workforce equipped with relevant technical and occupational competencies. Dr Adzroe stressed the need to strengthen collaboration between training institutions and industry to ensure that skills development aligned with the country’s economic priorities and labour market demands. Mr Sebastian Deh, Member of Parliament of Kpando, and Chairman of the Governing Council of the Ghana TVET Service, said more than 16 sector skills bodies had been activated to enable industry players to identify the skills required in their respective sectors. He urged TVET institutions to ensure that at least 50 per cent of practical training took place in industry, enabling learners to acquire hands-on experience in real workplace settings. Mr Deh also appealed to businesses to open their factories, garages, farms and construction sites to learners to strengthen practical training and bridge the gap between classroom instruction and industry requirements.

items.title: ECONOMY: The Missing Entrepreneur of Sindh
items.description: Fishermen pictured along the coast of Sindh: despite an abundance of agricultural produce, fisheries and traditional crafts, Sindh’s potential has not resulted in local businesses that could create jobs beyond agriculture | AFP During a recent visit to Borneo island in the Malay archipelago, I came across a shrimp farm on the coast of the rainforest-covered island, run by a Chinese woman entrepreneur. Using a seawater reservoir behind a mangrove forest, she had built a business exporting shrimp around the world. My mind drifted home to Pakistan’s 1,058-kilometre coastline, along Sindh and Balochistan. Why, I wondered, do we see so little aquaculture of this kind? I was reminded of a conversation I had with the owner of a hatchery recently established in Gharo in Sindh. He told me that one of his biggest worries was transporting the hatchlings quickly and safely to fish and shrimp farms in Muzaffargarh, Punjab. The irony struck me. The hatchery is in coastal Sindh, close to the sea and the Indus delta, yet its young fish and shrimp have to travel hundreds of kilometres inland to find farms. I asked him why people were not investing in fish and shrimp farming in Sindh? He did not have a clear answer, except to say that there were not enough investors and the business climate is also not supportive. But the lack of investors is not really an explanation. It is itself a question. The problem in rural Sindh may not be a lack of capital, but its concentration — and the failure to create the conditions in which small businesses can grow into industries Sindh has fertile land, a long coastline and a river, alongside abundant agricultural produce, livestock, fisheries and traditional crafts. Yet much of this potential has not translated into local processing, packaging and cold-chain businesses that could create jobs beyond agriculture. Why did this not happen? THE AGRARIAN DIVIDE Economic historian Imran Ali has documented how British canal colonies transformed western Punjab from the late 19th century. Irrigation brought semi-arid land under cultivation, encouraging commercial agriculture and the growth of new settlements and market towns. The colonial project also served revenue, political and military objectives. Regardless of their motives, the economic landscape was transformed. Sindh too underwent an irrigation revolution, particularly after the Sukkur Barrage opened in 1932. But perhaps the social structure on to which this new agricultural wealth was grafted was different. Economist Mahmood Hasan Khan points out the growth of small owner-cultivators and market relations in parts of Punjab, while the older landlord-sharecropper structure remained much stronger in Sindh. Economist Akmal Hussain argues that owner-cultivators have greater incentives to invest, potentially generating the savings and demand needed for industrialisation. Where agricultural income is concentrated in fewer hands, the pattern of investment may be different. THE CONCENTRATION OF CAPITAL It would, however, be too easy to explain Sindh’s predicament simply by invoking “feudalism.” Political economist Akbar Zaidi argues that agriculture in Pakistan has undergone a substantial capitalist transformation. Commercialisation and the ‘Green Revolution’ brought capitalist farmers, machinery and wage labour and, in some areas, small manufacturers, skilled workers and service businesses. Sindh’s sugar mills, cotton ginning and rice milling show that agricultural wealth did become industrial capital. But large enterprises owned by wealthy families are not the same as a broad base of independent businesses. Both represent investment and capitalism, but the latter creates a much wider entrepreneurial class. A farmer investing in transport, a workshop repairing agricultural machinery or a manufacturer producing spare parts can generate further demand for suppliers, traders and services. Why has this chain remained so weak across much of rural Sindh? THE CITY AND THE HINTERLAND Perhaps the problem was never simply the absence of capital. It may have been the concentration of capital and the failure to spread entrepreneurial investment widely enough through its towns and communities. And then there is Karachi. Economist Kaiser Bengali has described Sindh as having a “dual identity”: Karachi on one side and the rest of the province on the other. Partition created another rupture. Much of Sindh’s Hindu mercantile and entrepreneurial class migrated to India, while Muslim migrants from different parts of the Subcontinent brought new commercial skills, networks and capital to Karachi. Over the following decades, Karachi became Pakistan’s great port, financial centre and industrial metropolis. For someone from rural Sindh with money to invest, a good education or entrepreneurial ability, Karachi offered far greater opportunities than his own town. Perhaps herein lies another paradox. Sindh generated considerable wealth at both ends of its economy: agricultural wealth in the countryside and commercial and industrial wealth in Karachi. Yet the economic centres in between remained relatively weak. BEYOND INDUSTRIAL ESTATES History, however, can only explain so much. Nearly eight decades have passed since Independence, and we also have to ask what we have done since then. Why have Sukkur, Larkana, Nawabshah, Mirpurkhas, Khairpur, Thatta and Badin not developed stronger clusters of small industry? Industrial estates and special economic zones have been established or proposed outside Karachi, but infrastructure alone does not create an industrial ecosystem. Regional businesses also need technical training, accessible finance, shared processing and testing facilities, and reliable market connections. Perhaps the more fundamental question is why we wait for investors instead of creating the conditions that produce investors. THE MISSING STEP A recent article by journalist Owais Tohid about thousands of women establishing tiny businesses across rural Sindh provides an interesting clue. These women are raising livestock, stitching clothes, producing handicrafts and running other small businesses with relatively modest amounts of capital. Perhaps entrepreneurship was never absent. The problem is what happens next. How does a woman employing herself begin employing five or ten other women? How does a workshop become a factory? How does one successful shrimp farm become twenty, surrounded by hatcheries, feed suppliers, cold storage, processors, transporters and exporters? This brings me back to that hatchery in Gharo. The coastline is there, as are the seawater, the hatchery, the technical knowledge and the market. And yet the hatchlings travel hundreds of kilometres to find the entrepreneurs willing and able to farm them. Successive governments in Sindh must also bear part of the responsibility. A political economy historically dominated by large landowners may not have had sufficient incentive to create a broad class of independent entrepreneurs. Industrial estates have been established, but we have rarely pursued industrial development around the natural strengths of individual regions with the persistence it requires: dates in Khairpur, fisheries and aquaculture along the coast, rice in upper Sindh, fruit processing around Mirpurkhas, and livestock and dairy across much of the province. Nor can poverty alleviation alone be an economic policy. There is an obvious need for social protection in a province where millions remain poor. But cash support, however necessary, cannot by itself create economic mobility. The larger challenge is to create the conditions in which people can move beyond poverty. A tenant becoming an owner, a woman running a tiny business beginning to employ others, a workshop growing into a factory, or a farmer’s produce being processed and packaged before it leaves the district rather than being sent elsewhere for someone else to add value to it — these are perhaps better measures of economic development. The challenge for rural Sindh, therefore, may not simply be to find more investors. It is to understand why enterprise has failed to spread despite the province’s considerable natural resources and agricultural wealth, and then to create the conditions in which capital, skills and entrepreneurship can come together. Ultimately, the measure of development should not merely be how many poor people the state is able to support, but how many people are able to reach a point where they no longer need that support. The writer is an entrepreneur and President of WWF-Pakistan Published in Dawn, EOS, October 18th, 2026

items.title: CHASS demands prompt release of free SHS funds and payment of arrears
items.description: The Conference of Heads of Assisted Secondary Schools (CHASS) has urged the Government to release funds to senior high schools promptly, settle outstanding arrears and review tax and procurement measures it says are placing additional financial pressure on schools. The call was contained in a communiqué issued at the end of CHASS’s 64th Annual National Conference, held at Mawuli School in Ho, Volta Region, from October 11 to 17, 2026, on the theme: “Student Discipline in a Challenging World: Context, Challenges and a Constructive Way Forward.” The communiqué cited by the Ghana News Agency (GNA) was signed by Rev. Fr. Stephen Owusu-Sekyere, President of CHASS, and Mr Primus Baro, Secretary of the association. CHASS identified delays in the release of inadequate funds as its primary challenge, expressing concern that the situation persisted despite the establishment of a dedicated funding source for the Free Senior High School (Free SHS) programme, which the association had strongly advocated. It said the delays were undermining the effective administration of schools and called for a more reliable funding arrangement. The Association said it would no longer accept explanations based on discrepancies in school data to justify delays, recalling that funds for first-year students were withheld throughout the 2025/2026 academic year. It also called for the full payment of outstanding arrears, including legacy recurrent grants accumulated between 2021 and 2024, to enable schools to settle longstanding debts to suppliers and other creditors. On emergency food procurement, CHASS said heads of schools had been authorised by the Director-General of the Ghana Education Service (GES) to procure food items for students during November and December 2025, but the funds needed to pay the suppliers had yet to be released. The situation, it said, had left some suppliers pursuing school heads for payment, despite the procurement having been officially authorised. The association urged the Government to settle the outstanding food-procurement bills without further delay to ease the financial burden on school heads. It said the affected administrators should not be left to bear the consequences of unpaid obligations arising from purchases made under official instructions. CHASS also called for a review of measures involving Value Added Tax (VAT) on basic academic resources and the procurement of perishable food items, which it said were contributing to the financial difficulties facing schools. “We appeal to the Government to review these measures to ensure that adequate funds are available to schools,” the communiqué stated, adding that sufficient and timely funding was essential to effective school administration. The Association reaffirmed its commitment to improving student discipline and academic performance, stressing that school leaders needed adequate resources to deliver quality education. I t called on the Government to address the funding delays, clear the arrears, and review the procurement-related measures to enable schools to meet their obligations and focus on teaching and learning.

GMA seeks integration of maritime systems to boost trade facilitation
items.description: The Ghana Maritime Authority (GMA) has called for stronger coordination and integration of existing maritime information systems to improve trade facilitation and operational efficiency at the country’s ports. Dr Kamal‑Deen Ali, the Director-General of the Ghana Maritime Authority (GMA), said the integration of systems used by maritime, customs and port authorities was essential to building a more cohesive maritime transport ecosystem. Dr Ali was speaking at a three-day sub-regional stakeholder workshop on Maritime Single Windows and Port Community Systems, which brought together representatives of maritime administrations, customs agencies, port authorities, private industry and development partners. He said the workshop provided an opportunity for participating countries to share experiences and identify practical ways to strengthen their maritime systems in line with international requirements. The representative noted that the Maritime Single Window requirement under the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) took effect in 2024, making it important for countries to accelerate their implementation efforts. He stated that in Ghana, several institutions operated systems supporting different aspects of maritime transport, trade facilitation and safety. These included systems used by customs and port authorities for trade and vessel clearance, as well as the vessel traffic monitoring system operated by the GMA for maritime safety. He said the relationship between maritime trade and safety made coordination among the various systems particularly important. He added that rather than working in isolation, the systems needed to be refined and integrated to support more effective port operations and the smooth movement of maritime trade. He also highlighted existing inter-agency coordination arrangements in Ghana, including committees that brought together relevant institutions under the GMA’s leadership. The three-day workshop was expected to provide lessons from participating countries and other stakeholders to help Ghana and its regional partners develop more coherent maritime information systems. Dr Ali expressed optimism that the discussions would help build a more integrated Maritime Single Window framework in the coming years.
